Question three. Why can a sensitive test for a rare disease still give mostly false positives? Take ten thousand people. One percent are sick, so a hundred, and the test catches ninety-nine of them. It also flags five percent of the nine thousand nine hundred who are healthy. That's four hundred and ninety-five false alarms. So of five hundred and ninety-four positives, ninety-nine are sick. One in six, about seventeen percent. Ninety-nine percent was the sensitivity, measured only on the sick. To read a positive, you also need the false-positive rate on the healthy, and the base rate. Next, two ideas that are easy to mix up.

Question four. What does it mean for two events to be independent? Knowing one tells you nothing about the other: the probability of A given B is just the probability of A. Split a thousand users by plan. If churn didn't depend on the plan, both bars would break at the same height, fifteen percent. These break at six and twenty-four, so plan and churn are dependent. So treat independence as a claim to justify. Repeat visits by the same user, or network effects, break it. Question five. How is that different from mutually exclusive? Mutually exclusive events can't happen together, so the probability of both is zero. Roll a one, and you didn't roll a two. Knowing the first drops the second from one in six to zero, which is as far from independent as it gets. Then the two numbers that sum up a random variable.
